passage:
Playschool note, Thursday (Ms Joyce, Butterfly group)
At drawing time Afreen had the only box of glitter crayons. Jagdish asked first, and she handed him two at once, saying, "You gave me your sticker yesterday." When Bittu reached for one, Afreen covered the box with both arms. "No. You never give me." Bittu sat down hard and sulked. I knelt between them and said, "Afreen remembers who shared. Bittu, what could you share today?" Bittu offered his blue clay. Afreen took it and slid one crayon across 🙂
Next step: a sharing song before drawing tomorrow.

qa.q: What had Jagdish given Afreen yesterday?
qa.a: Jagdish had given Afreen a sticker yesterday.

qa.q: What does Afreen covering the box with both arms show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she feels cross with Bittu, because in her mind he never shares with her.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms Joyce turned the moment around?
qa.a: Instead of ordering Afreen to share, Ms Joyce asked Bittu what he could share, and his blue clay opened the way to a crayon.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Bittu to hear "You never give me"?
qa.a: Bittu might feel stung and shut out, which is why he sits down hard and sulks until he finds a way to join in.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never does.

passage: Behind the rice fields, under the big guava tree, Reena, five, had filled her frock pocket with guavas. Joseph came running. Yesterday he had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond. Reena held out the biggest guava straight away. "For you. You gave me." Then Kuttan came, the boy who always kept his mango slices behind his back. "Give me one." Reena shook her head hard. "You don't give. I don't give." Kuttan kicked at the mud. Reena's Ammachi, drying chillies on a mat nearby, called out, "Kuttan, bring your mango tomorrow, and see what happens."

qa.q: What did Joseph share with Reena yesterday?
qa.a: He had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond.

qa.q: Why did Reena shake her head hard at Kuttan?
qa.a: She felt cross: in her mind Kuttan never shares, so he hadn't earned a guava: "You don't give. I don't give."

qa.q: What does Ammachi's suggestion offer Kuttan, and why might it work?
qa.a: It gives Kuttan a way to earn a turn by bringing his mango tomorrow, which fits the way Reena thinks about fairness 🙂

qa.q: How might Kuttan feel watching Joseph get the biggest guava?
qa.a: Kuttan might feel left out and cross, and perhaps start to notice that hiding his mango has a cost.

grounding: A young child gives her best guava to the friend who shared with her and refuses the boy who never shares.

passage: In the small park near their flats in Cape Town, Siddiq, five, was pushing his new red digger through the sand. Thabo wandered over. Last Saturday Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back. "You can dig," Siddiq said, handing over the digger. Then Oliver from the swings came close, the boy who never let anyone touch his bucket. "My turn." Siddiq put a hand on the digger's scoop. "No. Thabo's turn. You never share your bucket." Oliver's face crumpled. On the bench, Siddiq's dad leaned forward. "What if Oliver lends the bucket?" Siddiq thought about it for a long time.

qa.q: What had Thabo let Siddiq ride last Saturday?
qa.a: Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq hand the digger to Thabo so quickly?
qa.a: He felt grateful for the scooter ride and thought Thabo deserved a turn back, like a fair swap.

qa.q: Was Dad's question a good way to handle the moment, and why?
qa.a: Yes; instead of forcing Siddiq to share, Dad offered Oliver a way into the "you give, I give" deal that Siddiq already believes in.

qa.q: How might Oliver see Siddiq's "You never share your bucket"?
qa.a: Oliver may feel hurt and surprised, perhaps realising for the first time that other children remember when he doesn't share.

grounding: A young child lends his toy to the friend who shared a scooter with him and refuses the child who never shares.

passage: In the office creche, Simran, five, had the animal puzzles. Kiran came over. Yesterday Kiran had given her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple. Simran pushed the box across at once. "You can do the lion. You gave me red." Then Babloo came, the boy who kept the blocks under his mat every day. "Give me the elephant." Simran put both hands on the box. "No. You never give me blocks." Babloo stamped his foot. The creche didi sat down. "Babloo, what could you share?" Babloo looked at his mat, then pushed two blocks over.

qa.q: What did Kiran give Simran yesterday?
qa.a: Kiran gave her the red crayon when she was colouring an apple.

qa.q: Why did Simran put both hands on the box when Babloo asked?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at the unfairness of giving to Babloo, who keeps the blocks under his mat every day and never shares.

qa.q: How did the creche didi help, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked Babloo what he could share, which let him see that giving makes others want to give back.

qa.q: How might Babloo feel when Simran refuses him?
qa.a: Babloo may feel angry and left out at first, which is why he stamps his foot, before realising he could share too.

grounding: A five-year-old shares with a friend who shared before and refuses a child who never shares, showing early 'you did for me, I do for you' fairness.

passage: I'm Charu, Mridul's big sister. On Sunday the building kids played in our hall. Mridul, five, had his new remote car. Guddu asked first. Last week Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages. Mridul gave him the remote at once. "You gave me bubbles, so you drive." Then Sonu stuck his hand out. Sonu never lets anyone touch his football. Mridul hid the remote. "No. You don't share, so I don't share." Sonu went red and sat by the door. Mridul kept looking at him. After Guddu's turn he walked over. "Bring your football next time."

qa.q: What had Guddu let Mridul do last week?
qa.a: Guddu had let Mridul blow his bubbles for ages.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been thinking when he kept looking at Sonu?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sorry for Sonu sitting alone, while still believing that sharing should go both ways.

qa.q: Which choice at the end helped, and why?
qa.a: Saying 'Bring your football next time' gave Sonu a way to join the give-and-take instead of being left out for good.

qa.q: How might Sonu feel sitting by the door?
qa.a: Sonu likely feels embarrassed and left out, seeing Guddu enjoy the car while he is refused.

grounding: A five-year-old shares his toy with a friend who shared before and refuses one who never shares, as told by his older sister.

passage: In the sandpit of a São Paulo park, Priscila, five, had the red dump truck. Yesterday Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon. Now Sami toddled over. Priscila pushed the truck straight to him. "Your turn!" Then Lucas came, the boy who never let anyone touch his digger. He reached for the truck. Priscila pulled it back. "No. You don't share." Lucas stamped. Priscila crossed her arms. "When you share, I share." She went back to building a sand road with Sami.

qa.q: Who had let Priscila use his bucket yesterday?
qa.a: Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she pulled the truck back from Lucas?
qa.a: Priscila felt it was unfair and a little cross, remembering that Lucas never let anyone touch his digger.

qa.q: What could a parent say to help all three children?
qa.a: A parent could praise Priscila for sharing with Sami and suggest Lucas try sharing his digger, so everyone sees how sharing works both ways.

qa.q: How might Lucas feel when Priscila said no?
qa.a: Lucas felt frustrated and left out, stamping his foot, maybe not yet understanding why.

grounding: A young child shares with the friend who shared last time and refuses the one who never shares, showing early "you did for me, I do for you" fairness.

passage: At Sunflower playschool, Uma, five, had the big box of crayons. Himani, who'd given Uma her pink crayon on Monday, sat down beside her. Uma slid the box over. "You can use all of them." Then Tinku came, the boy who always hid the glue stick in his pocket. He grabbed for the blue. Uma covered the box with both hands. "You never give me glue!" The teacher knelt down. "Tinku, what could you do?" Tinku slowly took the glue stick from his pocket and held it out. Uma thought, then pushed the blue crayon toward him.

qa.q: What did Tinku always hide in his pocket?
qa.a: He always hid the glue stick in his pocket.

qa.q: Why did Uma cover the box with both hands?
qa.a: Uma felt cross and wronged because Tinku never shared the glue, so she didn't want to share with him.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why did it work?
qa.a: The teacher asked Tinku what he could do, so he offered the glue and Uma was happy to share back.

qa.q: How might Himani feel when Uma slid the box over?
qa.a: Himani probably felt happy and included, since her kindness on Monday came back to her.

grounding: A young child shares crayons with the friend who shared before and refuses the one who never does, until he offers something back.

passage:
Monday: At the building playground, Parveen, five, let Sahil, six, have a long turn on her new swing seat. Sahil grinned.
Wednesday: Sahil brought his football. Parveen asked to kick it. "Yes! You gave me the swing." They played till dinner.
Friday: Bunty, who never lent his cycle to anyone, asked for the football. Sahil hugged it. "No. You never share." Bunty frowned and walked off. Sahil kicked the ball back to Parveen.

qa.q: What did Sahil bring on Wednesday?
qa.a: Sahil brought his football.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he hugged the ball on Friday?
qa.a: Sahil felt cross and wary because Bunty never shared his cycle, so he didn't want to share.

qa.q: What could help Bunty get a turn next time?
qa.a: Bunty could offer his cycle first, which would likely make Sahil want to share the football back.

qa.q: How did Parveen experience Sahil's sharing?
qa.a: Parveen felt happy and included, since her swing turn earlier was repaid with football.

grounding: Over a week, a young child shares with the friend who shared before and refuses the one who never does.

passage:
It was Holi morning, and Mummy said, "Five minutes, then we go to Nani's!" Vaibhav had one water pistol and no time.
His friend from upstairs held out a hand. Last Holi, that boy had shared all his green colour with Vaibhav. Vaibhav gave him the pistol at once. "You go first."
Then Lokesh came running. "Give me! Give me!"
Vaibhav hugged the pistol. "No. You never give me your cycle. Never."
"Please!"
"You didn't give, so I don't give." Vaibhav turned away.
Lokesh stamped his foot. Mummy called from the balcony. Time was up.

qa.q: What did the boy from upstairs share with Vaibhav last Holi?
qa.a: He shared all his green colour with Vaibhav.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav hug the pistol when Lokesh asked?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair to share with Lokesh, who never gives his cycle, so he felt stubborn and wanted to keep it.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Vaibhav and Lokesh next time?
qa.a: She could help them agree to take turns with the pistol and the cycle, so both learn that sharing goes both ways.

qa.q: What is it like for Lokesh when Vaibhav turns away?
qa.a: Lokesh feels angry and left out, and stamps his foot, maybe without knowing why Vaibhav won't share.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never shares, on a festival morning.

passage:
On a foggy winter afternoon in their Lucknow building, the children sat on the stairs with Himani's new crayons. Everyone wanted the gold one.
Noor had shared her glitter stickers with Himani last week. Himani held out the gold crayon to Noor first. "You gave me stickers. So you get gold."
A boy from the third floor reached for it next. He had a whole box of sketch pens and never let anyone touch them.
Himani pulled the crayons to her chest. "No. You never share your pens."
He sulked. Noor coloured a gold sun and gave the crayon back to Himani.

qa.q: What had Noor shared with Himani last week?
qa.a: Noor had shared her glitter stickers with Himani.

qa.q: How does Himani seem to feel about giving Noor the gold crayon first?
qa.a: She feels warm and fair-minded, happy to give back to the friend who gave to her.

qa.q: What could an adult say to the boy from the third floor?
qa.a: An adult could gently suggest that if he lets others try his sketch pens, they will want to share with him too.

qa.q: How might the boy from the third floor feel when Himani pulls the crayons away?
qa.a: He likely feels hurt and sulky, not yet seeing that his never sharing is the reason.

grounding: Shows a young child giving a treasured crayon to the friend who shared before and refusing the child who never shares.

passage:
"Nandini, give me the kite!"
"No, Dhruv."
"Why not?"
"Because you never give me the cycle. Never, not once, all summer."
"But the kite is fun!"
"The cycle is fun too."
"...If I give you the cycle, will you give me the kite?"
"Yes. You give, I give."
"Only one round."
"One round each."
"Okay. Here, take it. Don't fall."
Nandini rode to Nani's gate and back. Then she handed Dhruv the kite string.
"See?" she said. "Now it's fair." Dhruv grinned and ran off with his kite.

qa.q: What does Dhruv never give Nandini all summer?
qa.a: He never gives her the cycle.

qa.q: Why won't Nandini give Dhruv the kite at first?
qa.a: She feels it is unfair and a bit annoyed, because Dhruv never shares his cycle with her.

qa.q: What helped the two children share in the end?
qa.a: They agreed to swap one round each, so both got a turn and both gave something.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel after getting the kite string?
qa.a: Dhruv probably feels happy and learns that giving his cycle made Nandini willing to share.

grounding: Shows young children sharing on the rule "you give, I give" during the summer holidays.

passage: Playgroup note, rainy July week. Nazia had the block tub today. When Ojas came over, she tipped half the blocks toward him at once: "You gave me your red car yesterday." Then a boy who usually grabs and keeps things reached in. Nazia pulled the tub back. "No. You never give me." He started to cry. I sat with them both and said, "You remember who shares with you. That's fair thinking." Then I gave the boy a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first. He did. Nazia passed him two blocks. Next: more take-turns games.

qa.q: What did Ojas give Nazia yesterday?
qa.a: His red car.

qa.q: Why did Nazia pull the tub back from the other boy?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair, because he never gives her things; she was annoyed and protective of her blocks.

qa.q: What did the note-writer try next, and why could it help?
qa.a: The boy got a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first, so she saw him give and was willing to give back.

qa.q: What is it like for the boy when Nazia says "You never give me"?
qa.a: He feels hurt and left out, and cries, perhaps not yet understanding that his grabbing is why she won't share.

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing one who never does.

passage: Pongal morning, and the village square smelled of sweet rice. Madhuri spun her new paper pinwheel. Tanuja ran up. Yesterday Tanuja had shared her sugarcane. "Here, you blow," Madhuri said, holding it out. Then a bigger cousin came, the one who never let anyone touch his top. "Give!" Madhuri hid the pinwheel behind her. "You didn't give me your top." "So?" "So no." Her grandmother, shelling peanuts nearby, chuckled. "You keep good accounts, little one." The cousin sulked by the well. After a while he rolled his top toward Madhuri's feet. She blinked, then held out the pinwheel.

qa.q: What had Tanuja shared yesterday?
qa.a: Her sugarcane.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she said "So no"?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair to share with someone who never lets anyone touch his top; she was firm and a little cross.

qa.q: What changed the cousin's luck with the pinwheel?
qa.a: He rolled his top toward Madhuri first, and then she held out the pinwheel; giving first opened the door.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel while sulking by the well?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and annoyed, and perhaps began to see that sharing gets sharing back.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never shares.

passage: Christmas Eve in Madrid, with thin snow on the park hill. Last week Esther had let Santiago ride her sled three times, so today he waved her over to his red one. "You go first!" Esther whooped all the way down. Then a boy from the building next door marched up. He always kept his scooter to himself. "My turn." Santiago held the rope tight. "You never let me ride your scooter." "That's different." "No, it's the same." His papá said, "Maybe he'll share next time if you share now?" Santiago thought hard, then gave one turn. Just one.

qa.q: How many times had Esther let Santiago ride her sled last week?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Santiago hold the rope tight?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't fair, because the boy always kept his scooter to himself; Santiago was reluctant and a bit indignant.

qa.q: What did Santiago's papá suggest, and why is it a useful idea?
qa.a: That sharing now might lead to sharing next time; it shows the boy a chance to join in the give-and-take.

qa.q: How might Esther feel about being waved over first?
qa.a: She would feel pleased and liked, seeing that her sharing last week was remembered.

grounding: Illustrates a young child sharing with the friend who shared last time and holding back from one who never shares.

passage: On the first cold morning of December, the anganwadi floor is covered with a warm durrie, and the red truck is the best toy. Mridul, five, has it. Vishal comes over. Yesterday Vishal let Mridul hold his clay elephant. "Here," says Mridul, and pushes the truck across. Then Bunty holds out his hand. Bunty never shares his crayons, not even the broken ones. Mridul pulls the truck back to his chest. "No. You didn't give me yesterday." Bunty's lip trembles. The didi kneels down. "Hmm. What could Bunty do?" Bunty looks at his crayons.

qa.q: What did Vishal let Mridul hold yesterday?
qa.a: His clay elephant.

qa.q: Why does Mridul pull the truck back when Bunty asks?
qa.a: He feels it isn't fair and is a bit cross that Bunty never shares his crayons, so he only gives to the friend who gave to him.

qa.q: How does the didi handle it, and why is that a good idea?
qa.a: She asks what Bunty could do, helping the children see that sharing goes both ways without scolding anyone 🙂.

qa.q: What is it like for Bunty to be refused?
qa.a: Bunty feels hurt and close to tears, and starts to look at his own crayons in a new way.

grounding: A young child shares a toy with the friend who shared yesterday and refuses the one who never shares.
